summary:
Selangor stands under the national framework of Malaysia. At federal level, sections 377A to 377D of the Penal Code criminalise same-sex intimacy and "outrages on decency" with up to twenty years' imprisonment plus whipping; the Human Dignity Trust country profile, last updated 16 December 2025, records that these provisions have been enforced in recent years, apply to both men and women, and are usable against transgender people. They are not limited to Malaysian citizens and reach foreign visitors.

At state level, every one of the 13 states and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya maintains Sharia enactments criminalising cross-dressing or a man posing as a woman, with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. These offences reach Muslims only. Enforcement is carried out by state Islamic religious departments, and the enactments contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing.

Selangor is the state where the religious-enforcement apparatus has been most publicly exercised against gender expression. In 2021 the transgender cosmetics entrepreneur Nur Sajat failed to appear in a Selangor Sharia court to answer criminal charges of "insulting Islam" grounded in her attire; the state religious department issued a warrant for her arrest and announced that it had mobilised 122 religious-affairs officers to hunt her down, then sought her extradition from Thailand. She was permitted to remain under UNHCR protection and later settled in Australia. Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters, in a report released on 10 August 2022, cite the deployment as evidence of how far Malaysian authorities go to enforce rigid gender norms.

Litigation has narrowed the state layer without loosening the federal one. In 2021 the Federal Court struck down provisions of the Selangor Syariah Criminal Offences Enactment 1995 as exceeding state power, on federalism grounds; the Penal Code offences remain fully intact. A Selangor Sharia court has also sentenced five men to six to seven months' imprisonment with six strokes of the cane.

State-backed restriction is ongoing. A crackdown on LGBT people has run since the 2018 election, and at least 1,733 people had attended state "rehabilitation programmes" as of June 2021; Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters found such programmes to internalise discrimination and foment self-hatred.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor, the Selangor Sharia cross-dressing offences do not apply, but the Penal Code does. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the documented pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters documented investigations spanning Kuala Lumpur, Selangor, Negeri Sembilan, Kelantan, Penang, Pahang and Kedah, indicating that the enforcement pattern is national rather than confined to any one state. Sharia codes in the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya go further than cross-dressing provisions and criminalise same-sex activity as well as gender nonconformity.

The Sajat case shows the extraterritorial reach of the apparatus: a state religious department sought extradition of a transgender woman from Thailand, and she ultimately required UNHCR protection before settling in Australia. The federalism ruling that voided Selangor's 1995 enactment provisions did not touch the parallel federal Penal Code layer, so the removal of a state offence does not remove a visitor's exposure.
localsOnly:
Selangor residents who are Muslim remain subject to the state Sharia enactments on cross-dressing, punishable by up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning, enforced by the state Islamic religious department. Non-Muslim residents fall outside those offences but remain subject to the federal Penal Code.

The Federal Court's 2021 ruling voided provisions of the Syariah Criminal Offences Enactment 1995 as beyond state power, altering the state-level legal position for residents without affecting federal offences. Residents also face the state rehabilitation apparatus: at least 1,733 people had attended state "rehabilitation programmes" by June 2021, under a crackdown on LGBT people running since the 2018 election, and Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters found these programmes internalise discrimination and foment self-hatred.

Selangor Sharia courts have imposed custodial sentences with corporal punishment on same-sex conduct, including six to seven months' imprisonment with six strokes of the cane for five men. A transgender resident who fails to appear in court on Sharia charges risks an arrest warrant and large-scale officer deployment, as the 2021 warrant and the mobilisation of 122 religious-affairs officers in the Sajat case demonstrate.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Selangor provisions struck down by the Federal Court in 2021 have been re-enacted in amended form is not addressed in the sources reviewed here.

The current status of the "insulting Islam" charges that produced the 2021 warrant against Nur Sajat, and whether any further extradition request remains live, is unresolved in these sources.

Whether the state "rehabilitation programmes" recorded at 1,733 attendees by June 2021 are still running, and at what scale, is not sourced beyond that date.

The frequency with which sections 377A to 377D are actually enforced against foreign visitors in Selangor is not quantified in the inventory; the assessment that tourists are rarely targeted rests on the raid-based pattern described in the national framework rather than on Selangor-specific arrest statistics.

Whether the 122-officer deployment announced in the Sajat case remains standing policy of the Selangor religious department is not stated in these sources.
